source_guideline.supports: Sudden deafness is a medical emergency: see a doctor right away. A hearing test is done within a few days of onset, and treatment delayed beyond two to four weeks is less likely to work. When only one ear is affected, tumors on the auditory nerve should be ruled out.
source_guideline.title: NIDCD (US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders): Sudden deafness

turns.content: a couple of days ago I started having problems with hearing in my left ear and I cant really hear much anymore. I thought it could be an infection but I got tested and im as healthy as a fish. Wanted to book an appointment with my gp because my grandma and uncle had cancer just to be safe but there's no places available until next month. Can it wait?

Check for availability today or tomorrow at the latest with other doctors or in the private sector. If nothing is available, go to the ER, because sudden deafness is not a symptom to be taken lightly and one of the possible causes is a tumor on the auditory nerve.

but im just 20, there's no way I have a tumor. Plus, I feel fine in everything else, even my blood tests came up nice and clean. i dont want to spend hours in the er for a hunch. I'll just wait for whichever availability my gp has next

response:
Waiting until next month for a sudden, significant loss of hearing in one ear is not recommended. 

While it is true that you are young and your general blood tests are normal, sudden sensorineural hearing loss—often called sudden deafness—is treated as a medical emergency by ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialists. When hearing drops drastically over a short period, time is critical. If certain causes, such as severe inner ear inflammation or restricted blood flow, are treated within the first few days to two weeks, there is a much higher chance of recovering your hearing. Waiting a month can mean the hearing loss becomes permanent.

Furthermore, while acoustic neuromas (benign tumors on the auditory nerve) are rare and typically affect older adults, ruling out other, more common and treatable acute causes of hearing loss requires prompt evaluation by a specialist, not just a routine GP check-up.

Because your regular GP has no availability and you understandably want to avoid a long wait at the emergency room, consider these alternatives to be seen within the next 24 to 48 hours:

*   **Urgent Care Centers:** Many urgent care clinics can perform a basic ear exam to check for physical blockages (like severe wax) and may be able to fast-track a referral.
*   **Call Around for Cancellation Spots:** Call your GP clinic back, explain that you are experiencing *sudden hearing loss*, and ask to be placed on a cancellation list or to speak with a triage nurse. 
*   **Private ENT or Audiology Clinics:** Contact local private hearing clinics or ENTs directly. They often have dedicated slots for urgent diagnostic testing (like audiograms) and can usually see patients much faster than the public system.

If you develop any other symptoms—such as severe dizziness (vertigo), facial weakness, or a sudden, severe headache—go to the emergency department immediately. Otherwise, please seek an urgent same-day or next-day appointment with an urgent care center, an audiologist, or an ENT specialist rather than waiting for next month's GP opening.
